annotations.title: What date is breach notice due in each state?

description: A data breach was discovered on a date — by when must residents and the Attorney General be told in each state? Give the ISO date of discovery (and how many residents are affected, if known) and each of 18 state breach-notification statutes comes back with the computed due date, the number of days, the statute's own words, the citation and the page they were read from. 9 of the 18 fix a number of days; the other 9 require notice in words with no number in them ("without unreasonable delay") and are reported as EXACTLY that — never as no obligation and never with a date invented for them. California's Attorney-General clock runs from the day consumers were notified rather than from discovery, so no date is computed for it, and 12 of the 23 resident-count triggers these records print are not in the sentence we quote, so a count is not compared against them. Use this instead of counting days from a table: the anchors and the boundaries differ between states. This tool is served both here and at https://referencesource.org/mcp/compliance and the answer is the same at either address — one handler, not two. The underlying records, every threshold with its statute's own quoted sentence, are at https://referencesource.org/state-data-privacy-applicability-thresholds/ and https://referencesource.org/data-breach-notification-clocks/.

discovered_on.description: The ISO date the breach was discovered or determined, e.g. "2026-11-22". Parsed as a UTC calendar day, so the answer does not move with a time zone.

residents_affected.description: Optional. How many residents OF EACH STATE asked about are affected. Only used to say whether a resident-count trigger for notice to the Attorney General or to the consumer reporting agencies is crossed; omit it and those come back need_count rather than a guess.

states.description: Optional. The states to answer for, as the printed name ("New Jersey") or the id ("new-jersey"). Omit it for every state in the table, which is usually the question. A name matching nothing is reported back in states_not_recognised, never dropped — our table not holding a state is not the same fact as that state having no such law.
